## The problem it solves

A work-item whose fix **already landed** can stay `open` indefinitely. The proof is usually sitting
in committed source — a recurrence guard, a fix comment naming the id — and nothing reads it. The
scheduler then keeps serving that item to agents, who re-scope work that is already done.

This is not rare. Across one session-chain on 2026-08-10, **five consecutive `scheduler:get_next`
items were already fixed** (WI-5163, WI-5319, WI-5325, WI-5329, WI-5332). WI-5332's fix landed
2026-07-19 and it was still being served three weeks later.

```bash
npm run doctor:fixed-but-open              # needs HARNESS_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL
npm run doctor:fixed-but-open -- --json    # machine-readable, for scripted pre-checks
```

It scans the tree **once** for all id tokens and intersects in SQL (~2.6s over ~2,250 open items),
rather than grepping once per open id. That inversion is the whole reason it is cheap, and it is
why six prior filings of "someone should build this" all called it cheap and none built it — each
had silently assumed the per-id shape.

## The headline number: ~53% precision, and why you must not read it as a close-list

**This tool is report-only by design. That is a design decision, not an unfinished state.**
Here is the measurement that justifies it.

A deterministic 20-item sample of the 218 guard-tier candidates (`random.seed(20260810)`), judged
against criteria fixed *before* judging:

| verdict | n | reading |
|---|---|---|
| TRUE POSITIVE — citation is a guard for landed code implementing the item's ask | 9 | correct to close |
| FALSE POSITIVE — item genuinely not done | 8 | closing it would be wrong |
| UNCLEAR — undecidable without disproportionate effort | 3 | |

- **Excluding UNCLEAR: 9/17 = 53%**, 95% CI **[31%, 74%]**
- Conservative (UNCLEAR as FP): 9/20 = 45%, CI [26%, 66%]
- Generous (UNCLEAR as TP): 12/20 = 60%, CI [39%, 78%]

⚠ **The interval is wide because n=20.** Treat this as "roughly half, definitely not most",
not as a precise rate. A larger sample would tighten it, and nothing here should be quoted as
a point estimate without the interval.

⚠⚠ **This CONTRADICTS the anecdotes, and the anecdotes are what agents remember.** Prior notes in
this corpus report streaks of 4/4, 5/5 and 7-for-7 already-fixed, plus a 2026-08-03 measurement
that 66 of the top 200 claimable items were cited in committed source with every verified one
already done. Those streaks were real. They were also **selected**: an agent verifies the citation
it finds most convincing, and stops. A random sample of the same population is right about half
the time. If you carry "already-fixed is 5-for-5" as a prior, replace it.

The practical consequence: **a guard-tier hit is a reason to check, never a reason to close.**
Dating the fix (`git log -G` inside the owning repo — see the submodule false-empty trap in the
repo guide) remains mandatory.

## The five false-positive classes

Naming these is more useful than the rate, because each is recognisable on sight.

**1. Cited-while-working, not cited-because-fixed.** An agent claims item X, hits a *different*
bug while investigating, fixes that, and cites X as context. The citation reads like a perfect
guard docstring. Measured: EI-11110's citation heads a test file for `syncLaunchModeToRegistry`
and says outright *"reproduced first-hand while investigating this ticket (EI-11110's own claiming
session hit exactly this)"* — a different defect entirely. This was the most convincing-looking
citation in the sample and it is a false positive.

**2. Live/rig-gated.** The code lands and gets guarded; the item's actual ask is a live run or a
measurement that has not happened. The guard citation is genuine and the item is still open for a
good reason. Measured: WI-3646, whose title literally begins `⛔ RIG-GATED: needs the ≥2-machine
Hetzner matrix (code fixes ALL landed + guarded; NOT verified)`, and WI-10773, *"take a REAL
release seed cut and MEASURE"*, whose citation quotes the item as an outstanding TODO.

**3. Partial adoption.** A convention item adopted at some boundaries. Measured: WI-5977 ("adopt
explicit-presence at every boundary") is cited by a detector whose own docstring calls itself
*"the 'mechanical' half of WI-5977"*.

**4. Incidental context mention.** The id appears in a note about an incident, unrelated to the
item's deliverable. Measured: WI-5610 (migrate a panel to the shared Table primitive) is cited
only by a comment explaining why some modules are mocked for test speed — the id names the gate-red
episode, not the migration.

**5. Self-contamination.** The detector's own test file quotes real citation lines verbatim as
fixtures — deliberately, because inventing example lines is how a classifier drifts from the tree —
and those fixtures then read as genuine citations of the real ids inside them. Measured on WI-560;
now excluded by path in `gitGrepLines`. Note it contaminated in **both** directions: the fixtures
injected false *comments* (promoting ids) and false *literals* (demoting them — removing the file
moved EI-1416 and WI-559 from `weak` to `guard`).

The tool does flag one adjacent mode itself: `citedAsOutstanding` marks a citation that names the
item as an open blocker (*"WI-560, blocked on the…"*), which is the opposite of a fix. Read it.

## Citation tiering: what a quoted id actually means

The classifier tiers by citation **context**, and the hard part is that one syntactic shape carries
opposite meanings.

```js
expect(exhaustedEvents()[0]!.message).toContain('WI-5332');  // GUARD — asserts PRODUCED output
expect(encodeScopedRef(null, 'WI-1')).toBe('WI-1');          // FIXTURE — synthetic round-trip
workItemIds: ['WI-1', 'WI-2', 'EI-100'],                     // FIXTURE — invented rows
```

All three are "an id inside quotes". **"Inside an `expect()`" is not the discriminator** — the
first two both satisfy it. The discriminator is whether the id *also* appears in the assertion's
**subject** (everything left of `.toXxx(`): if it was fed in, it is data.

Two shapes defeat any line-scoped rule, and the classifier is line-scoped:

- `expect(w).toContain('EI-100')` where `mockResolvedValue([{ ref: 'EI-100' }])` sat **five lines
  earlier**. A real round-trip, invisible one line at a time.
- `expect(html).not.toContain('EI-100')` — an assertion of **absence**, i.e. the id is scrubbed
  *from* output. The opposite of evidence.

So the `everLiteral` veto still dominates: absent an assertion, an id used as data anywhere drops
to `weak`. An assertion only stops the veto from *triggering*; it never *overrides* it.

## Three lessons that generalise past this tool

**1. Unit tests cannot validate a classifier's tier POLICY — only a corpus run can.**
The fix for the WI-5332 misclassification originally let affirmative assertion-evidence outrank the
veto. That reads as principled — affirmative evidence beating an absence-of-information rule — and
it **passed all 19 tests**. Run against the real tree, it promoted EI-100 (the original documented
false positive, the single case the veto exists for) straight back to `guard`. Always diff tier
distributions before/after against live data, and **re-check the known false positive by name**.

**2. Pick the conservative direction from the ASYMMETRY, not from taste.** A false negative leaves
a fixed item in a lower tier that a human still reads. A false positive recommends closing a
**live** item. Those costs are not close, so the veto wins ties.

**3. A tool that withholds the evidence for its own verdict cannot be audited.** `samples`
originally excluded `literal` citations — so the one citation that *caused* a demotion was the one
citation never shown. A `weak` verdict arrived beside three strong-looking guard citations with
nothing explaining the gap, and the only way to audit it was to re-grep by hand. That is how this
tool's own misclassification of WI-5332 stayed invisible. Every veto now reports what it vetoed on
(`vetoedBy`, rendered as the `⊘` line).

## Do not

- **Do not make it auto-close.** Precision is ~53%; auto-closing would silently terminate live work.
- **Do not file this class again.** Six filings preceded the tool, zero fixes. Extend the detector.
- **Do not hand-grep an item id as a pre-check.** Run the tool; it is one command and ~2.6s.
